questions.title: Standard of review for DuPont factors: Question of law or question of fact?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the standard of review in this case. The court says that 'likelihood of confusion is a question of law,' but then says that 'each of the [thirteen] DuPont factors presents a question of fact' which is reviewed for 'substantial evidence.' If the ultimate conclusion is a question of law (de novo), why are the individual factors treated as findings of fact? How does the court reconcile these two different standards in a single analysis?

questions.title: How can services be 'legally identical in part' if the parties provide different services?
questions.question_body: In this opinion, Apex Bank argues that they provide banking services and CC Serve provides credit card services, and that they aren't directly competitive. However, the court affirmed the Board's finding that the services are 'legally identical, in part.' I don't understand how two different business models (a retail bank vs. a credit card service provider) can be considered 'legally identical' just because a dictionary definition of 'banking' includes extending credit. Is this a common way the Board defines service similarity?

questions.title: What is the 'crowded field' theory and how does it affect a mark's 'scope of protection'?
questions.question_body: The court discusses the sixth DuPont factor and mentions that if a field is 'crowded with similar marks,' the mark is considered 'relatively weak' and entitled to a 'narrow scope of protection.' I'm struggling to understand the logic here: why does the existence of other similar marks make a mark weaker? Shouldn't it prove that the word (in this case, 'Aspire') is a common industry term and therefore less likely to cause confusion?

questions.title: Why is the Board prohibited from using different standards of 'similarity' for different DuPont factors?
questions.question_body: The court vacated the Board's finding on the sixth factor because the Board used a very broad definition of similarity for the second factor (banking $\approx$ credit cards) but a very narrow definition for the sixth factor (only counting marks specifically for credit card services). Is there a general rule that the definition of 'similar goods/services' must be consistent across all DuPont factors, or is this a specific error made by the Board in this case?

questions.title: Relationship between the Sixth Factor (Third-Party Use) and the First Factor (Commercial Impression)
questions.question_body: I don't understand why the court vacated the analysis of the first DuPont factor (similarity of the marks' appearance/sound/connotation) based on the error in the sixth factor (third-party use). The first factor seems to be about comparing the two marks at issue (ASPIRE vs. ASPIRE BANK), while the sixth is about other people's marks. Why does a change in the number of third-party marks change the 'commercial impression' of the marks in the specific dispute?
